lead: Ultrasonic (piezo) rhinoplasty is a way of performing the bone work of nose surgery with piezoelectric instruments rather than chisels, saws and rasps. People choose it to reshape the nose, for example by smoothing a dorsal hump, narrowing the bony vault or straightening the bridge, with the aim of a nose that sits in better harmony with the rest of the face. Surgeons who use it describe controlled, precise bone cuts that spare surrounding soft tissue [1][2].

A 2023 review of ultrasonic rhinoplasty and septoplasty states that the instruments allow precise osteotomies under direct visual control after an open or extended closed approach, as well as ostectomies and rhinosculpture, and that they preserve bone stability by not damaging support structures and avoiding unwanted fractures [1]. A 2024 comparison of mechanical, piezoelectric and electric instruments in the bony vault notes that mechanical instruments can cause radiating and comminuted fractures, and that piezoelectric instruments are selective, unlike electric ones [5].

A general rhinoplasty reference dates the introduction of ultrasonic rhinoplasty to 2004 and credits it to Massimo Robiony; it describes the devices as similar to those used in dental surgery and sparing of soft tissue [2]. Published comparative evidence is limited, and a registered randomised trial compares piezo and endonasal osteotomy [3].

angle.text: The technique is used during rhinoplasty to reshape the nasal bones: removing or lowering a hump, narrowing the bridge and repositioning the bony pyramid. Surgeons describe the instruments as giving fine control over where bone is cut and how far it moves [1].

infobox: Open or extended closed, to see the bony vault [1][2]

paras: The 2023 review frames the technique as applicable to dorsum preservation and to dorsum structural reconstruction, and says it gives control over nasal bone cuts, their orientation and the final position of the bones [1]. The general reference adds that it requires a more extensive surgical approach than some closed techniques, so the surgeon can see the whole bony vault [2].

In conventional rhinoplasty, Wikipedia describes the bony part of a dorsal hump being chiselled with an osteotome and smoothed with rasps, with the cut bones then realigned [2]. Piezo inserts are used in place of these tools for cuts and smoothing. The reviewers of bony vault instruments compare blunt mechanical, electric and piezoelectric tools on the commonest procedures performed on the nasal pyramid [5].

Piezosurgery uses ultrasonic vibration of a tip to cut mineralised tissue. Wikipedia reports that the technique was patented by Fernando Bianchetti, Domenico Vercellotti and Tomaso Vercellotti and was first used clinically in 1988; the tip vibrates over a small range at ultrasonic frequency, allowing selective cutting of bone that leaves soft tissue untouched [6]. It is mainly used in orthodontics, oral and craniofacial surgery [6]. Rhinoplasty adopted it for nasal bones and stiff cartilage, with the reshaping called rhinosculpture [2].

Wikipedia credits Massimo Robiony with introducing ultrasonic rhinoplasty in 2004 as an alternative to traditional bone instruments [2]. The broader history of nasal surgery stretches back to reconstructive work attributed to Sushruta in around 600 BC [7]; piezo instruments are a recent addition to a long tradition of nasal bone and cartilage surgery. Reviews from the 2020s describe piezoelectric cutting alongside preservation-style approaches such as dorsum preservation [1].

Specific safety data for piezo rhinoplasty are limited in the references available. Rhinoplasty in general carries risks that Wikipedia lists, including swelling that can take at least a year to fully resolve, deformities such as pollybeak, saddle nose and open roof deformity, and revision rates of 5 to 20 percent for rhinoplasties overall; smoking impairs healing [2]. Closed rhinoplasty is linked there to less postoperative swelling [2]. The bone-instrument review identifies fractures and surface defects as problems associated with mechanical osteotomies that piezoelectric instruments aim to reduce [5].

No completed head-to-head trials are summarised in the reviews cited here. A registered trial of 60 patients (status unknown, begun 2023) compares piezo and endonasal osteotomy methods on postoperative healing in septorhinoplasty [3]. A registered trial of photobiomodulation for swelling after rhinoplasty is recruiting and is not specific to piezo technique [4]. The two review articles describe the instruments and compare them narratively rather than reporting patient-level outcome data [1][5].

name: Ultrasonic (piezo) rhinoplasty

card.summary: Nose surgery that reshapes bone with piezoelectric ultrasonic tools instead of chisels and rasps; evidence is thin and mostly descriptive.
card.note: Few comparisons have been published; the available literature is a technique overview and two registered trials.

quick.overview:
Ultrasonic or piezo rhinoplasty uses instruments driven by piezoelectric vibration to cut and shape the nasal bones. Proponents describe more precise bone cuts and less collateral damage than hand chisels.
It is introduced in the literature as a bone-sculpting tool within otherwise standard rhinoplasty and is used in dorsal preservation work as well.
quick.mechanism: The instruments vibrate at ultrasonic frequency and cut bone while sparing soft tissue. A technique overview says they allow precise osteotomies under direct visual control after an open or extended closed approach, plus ostectomies and rhinosculpture.
quick.risks: Published work describes technique rather than comparative harms. A registered trial compares piezo with endonasal osteotomy on postoperative healing; its results have not been published.
